title: AI and Learning
text:
I use AI as a partner in teaching and learning, not as a replacement for either. The teacher still runs the lesson, and the student still does the work of learning. AI can help keep a record of the lesson, prepare for the next one, and give students structure for the practice they do on their own, when no teacher is in the room.


I started building this portal in 2024 for my own voice students. I now use it with all of my private students, and in 2026 it won the Pan American Vocology Association’s Best Microworkshop/ToolTalk award.
Try the demo Visit the studio portal
The demo uses sample student data, so you can look through lesson briefs, practice plans, and progress tracking without an account.


 Dashboard


 Lesson debrief and reflection


 Practice plan and log





Transcribes lessons and summarizes what we worked on and how the student responded
Prepares a brief before each lesson from the student’s past lessons, reflections, and repertoire
Writes an individual practice plan after each lesson
Gives students a web page where they can see their progress, reflections, and plans




It is written in Python and uses the Claude API from Anthropic, with Supabase for the database and logins. The AI’s instructions are based on my teaching framework, including the co-investigation model, motor learning phases, an exercise taxonomy, and safety guidelines.




I built a public archive of the graduate research from Boston Conservatory’s vocal pedagogy program. It holds 33 studies from 2022 to 2026 across 17 topics. Readers can search the catalog, follow a topic across cohorts, and explore the data in interactive figures. It is meant for students planning their own studies and for teachers looking for research they can bring into their studios. All data are confidentialized under Berklee’s institutional review board. I built the archive with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, and I maintain it with Claude as well.
Go to the research archive




Most of what happens in a lesson is never written down, and students forget much of it by the next week. The portal keeps a record that the student and teacher can both go back to. Graduate theses have a similar problem, since few people read them once they are filed, so the archive makes them public and searchable. I expect AI tools like this to become a normal part of teaching, and I think teachers should be involved in building them.



Ian Howell, Theodora Nestorova, and I talked about AI and teaching on the VocalFri Podcast in April 2026:





I’m open to consulting and advisory work with companies building learning technology and with schools rethinking how teachers are trained.

title: About
text:
I’m a mezzo-soprano, voice teacher, scholar, and program leader. At Boston Conservatory at Berklee, where I’m Assistant Professor of Voice and Vocal Pedagogy, I lead the graduate vocal pedagogy area and supervise graduate students’ research.


I studied vocal performance at San Diego State University and began teaching voice privately in 2012. While I was still a student, I co-founded the Folklore Guild, a choir that sang video game and film music, and I spent three years as Director of Development and Education for Bach Collegium San Diego. There I helped double the ensemble’s annual budget and used grants from the National Endowment for the Arts and the City of San Diego to start open rehearsals and lectures for students in Title I schools. It was my first time building an education program from the ground up.

   





I moved to Boston for a master’s degree in vocal pedagogy at New England Conservatory and stayed on in two jobs at once: Assistant Vocal Pedagogy Director on the faculty, and manager of the Voice and Sound Analysis Lab. Since 2019 I have been on the faculty of the Acoustic Vocal Pedagogy Workshop, now run by the Embodied Music Lab, and have helped organize it. When the pandemic moved lessons online, Ian Howell and I ran SoundJack Bootcamp to help musicians rehearse together over the internet and published a comparison of audio quality on the major video-call platforms.
At the same time I worked as a research assistant at the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) Voice Center on a study of ambulatory voice monitoring.



Boston Conservatory hired me in 2022 to lead the research side of two graduate degrees in voice teaching and singing, and to help students build their skills in scholarly reading, research, and publication. Since then we have built a voice science lab and a thesis sequence in quantitative and mixed methods with institutional review board (IRB) review for every study. I have also strengthened the conservatory’s existing partnership with the MGH Voice Center, which gives incoming voice students a screening and follow-up care. Student theses are collected in a public research archive.
In 2024 I took on leadership of the whole area, which includes the MM in Vocal Pedagogy and the MFA in Musical Theater Vocal Pedagogy. Alumni of the program have given 35 conference presentations since 2022, 19 of them at the Voice Foundation’s annual symposium, and graduates now teach at Oberlin, Brown, Catholic University of America, Oklahoma State, and UMass Amherst. I also direct the Vocal Pedagogy Professional Workshop for working voice teachers. In 2023 the National Association of Teachers of Singing (NATS) gave me its Voice Pedagogy Award.



 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
I call my approach scientific method informed voice teaching. In a lesson, I listen and watch, the student tells me what they feel, and we decide together what to try next. We keep what turns out to be observable, measurable, and repeatable. Over time I want students to be able to run these experiments on their own.
I tell my graduate students that research is a form of artistic expression, and that the best questions in voice research come from what teachers notice in their own studios. I talked about all of this on the VocalFri Podcast in 2025:





In 2024 I started building the AI Supported Voice Studio Portal, which I now use with my private students. After each lesson it produces a debrief and a practice plan, and students use it to track their progress between lessons. In 2026 it won the Pan American Vocology Association’s Best Microworkshop/ToolTalk award. More about the portal.
I want good voice pedagogy training to be available to teachers who cannot move to a conservatory city or pay conservatory tuition, and most of what I build now is meant for them.



I present regularly at the Voice Foundation Symposium, the Pan American Vocology Association, and the National Association of Teachers of Singing, usually with the graduate students whose research I supervise. Recent work includes:

Meikle, Brianna, Kayla Gautereaux, et al. “Performance Anxiety and Co-Regulation in the Vocal Audition.” Voice Foundation Symposium, May 2026.

I perform as a soloist and in choirs, and I sang backup for Ellie Goulding’s “Still Falling for You” at the 2022 Earthshot Prize Awards in Boston, with the Prince and Princess of Wales in the audience.

title: Teaching
text:
Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee


I lead two graduate degrees.


A 36-credit degree for singers who want to learn the science and craft of voice teaching, with pedagogy training in classical, musical theater, and contemporary styles.



A 60-credit terminal degree for teachers who specialize in musical theater. It includes an original thesis.




Research is built into both degrees. Since 2022 we have set up:

a voice science lab with acoustic analysis in Praat, heart rate and respiration monitoring, and Python data pipelines
a thesis sequence in quantitative and mixed methods, with review by an institutional review board (IRB) for every study
a public research archive of 33 graduate studies

The program also has a clinical partnership with the MGH Voice Center at Massachusetts General Hospital that predates my time here, and I have worked to strengthen it. Incoming voice students receive a voice screening, and those with findings receive physician follow-up.
MFA students design and carry out their own studies. Since 2022, alumni of the program have given 35 conference presentations, including 19 at the Voice Foundation, 7 at the Pan American Vocology Association, and 6 at the National Association of Teachers of Singing (NATS). Graduates teach at Oberlin Conservatory, Catholic University of America, Oklahoma State University, UMass Amherst, Brown University, and other schools.




 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
I direct the Vocal Pedagogy Professional Workshop (VPPW), a four-day summer workshop for voice teachers, with faculty from several institutions. Since 2019 I have also been on the faculty of the Acoustic Vocal Pedagogy Workshop, run by the Embodied Music Lab, and have helped organize it.



 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
I teach voice lessons and coach voice teachers privately, in person in the Boston area or online.
Visit the studio site
